Unlike prior upper-bound-based formulations, we obtain an exact quantification of which-path knowledge for the discrimination strategies considered here, encompassing previous strategies and extending beyond them. A general optimal measurement is implemented through a state-separation map governed by a continuous parameter $\xi\in[0,1]$, followed by minimum-error (ME) discrimination of either the successful outputs only (standard approach) or both successful and failure outputs (concatenated approach). Our framework identifies a strategy-dependent hierarchy that generally emerges in the tightness of the resulting duality relations. At $\xi=0$, both approaches reduce to the ME measurement, which typically yields the tightest relation. For $\xi>0$, each approach yields a distinct relation that generally becomes less tight as $\xi$ increases, with the concatenated strategy always yielding a relation at least as tight as its standard counterpart. We further characterize saturation of these relations by identifying the detector-state sets that lead to it and show that nontrivial saturation occurs only for interferometers with a nonprime number of paths. From these sets, we elucidate how the underlying structure of the quanton-detector correlations gives rise to this behavior and explains the lack of universal saturation in multipath duality relations for pure states.
item.dc:creator: L. F. Melo, O. Jim\'enez, L. Neves

item.title: A Route to Quantum-Coherent Thermodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2602.12212v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Equilibrium thermodynamics emerges because a vast number of microscopic states become indistinguishable at the level of local observables. We start from the observation that a nonequilibrium quantum state can also be represented by an ensemble of pure states that minimizes the average energy variance. We show that varying the statistical weights within this optimal family organizes state space into ``minimum-variance leaves'', which generalize the space of stationary states underlying equilibrium. We observe thermodynamic compression on the leaves, which in the simplest scenario manifests itself in the indistinguishability of states with the same energy density. We call this ``leaf typicality''; at equilibrium it reduces to eigenstate thermalization or its generalizations. Numerical tests support leaf typicality on some leaves and indicate a breakdown of its stronger forms on others, suggesting a rich thermodynamic organization beyond equilibrium. These results open a route to a unified statistical mechanics of equilibrium and nonequilibrium quantum states.
item.dc:creator: Maurizio Fagotti

item.title: Tight Quantum Speed Limit for Ergotropy Charging in the N-Qubit Dicke Battery
item.description: arXiv:2603.10415v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We derive a quantum speed limit for ergotropy charging in the $N$-qubit Dicke battery. With the qubits initially in their ground state and the charger in a coherent state of mean photon number $\bar{n}$, the charging time to a target fraction $\varepsilon$ of the maximum extractable work obeys, in the classical-field limit, $\Gamma_N \tau^{*}(\varepsilon) \geq \arcsin\sqrt{\varepsilon}$, where $\Gamma_N = 2\lambda\sqrt{\bar{n}/N}$ is a single rate combining the light-matter coupling, the charger amplitude and the system size. The bound is geometric: although the ergotropy is defined by an optimisation over unitaries, it reduces to a fixed function of the angle swept by the collective spin on the Bloch sphere, and the drive bounds the rate at which that angle can grow, so the charging time is at least the required arc divided by the maximum angular velocity. The reduction rests on an exact statement about work extraction: only the coherent component of the drive delivers extractable work, while its vacuum fluctuations deposit energy that remains locked in the passive state. This makes the short-time coefficient independent of the charger occupation, and it is what separates a bound on extractable work from a bound on stored energy, which no instantaneous-power argument can supply. At finite charger occupation the inequality is tested rather than proved: numerical integration of the full Dicke Hamiltonian, with a dynamical charger and a mixed battery state, finds the bound respected at every admitted charging time for two to five qubits, and approached most closely in the limit of small target work. The familiar square-root estimate is the chord to this arc, recovered in the small-angle limit and weaker whenever a large fraction of the maximum work is required.
item.dc:creator: Anass Jad, Abderrahim El Allati

item.title: Deterministic feedforward-based generation of large optical coherent-state superposition
item.description: arXiv:2603.22068v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large optical coherent-state superpositions are essential to advance quantum sensing, quantum repeaters and error-correction codes. We propose a deterministic feedforward protocol employing qubit-mode dispersive coupling, currently available in cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED). We show this single-mode protocol to outperform the advanced three-mode Gaussian-photon-number-resolving detector scheme both in terms of average fidelity and quantum non-Gaussian phase-space properties, and propose sensitivity to weak displacements of interference fringes as a feasible and conclusive witness of quantum interference. This approach combining QED with electro-optical feedforward is extendable to tailored states for applications and other platforms.
item.dc:creator: Michele N. Notarnicola, Marcin Jarzyna, Radim Filip

item.title: Quantum Algorithms for Gibbs Expectation of Non-log-concave and Heavy-tailed Distributions
item.description: arXiv:2604.00656v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We establish a systematic framework of unbiased quantum sampling and estimation protocols for the classical Gibbs expectation. This framework generalizes existing approaches to the partition function estimation and has broader applications in various fields. We consider sampling and estimation for a wide class of non-log-concave distributions, particularly heavy-tailed ones, under relaxed assumptions beyond strong convexity, such as dissipativity. We develop an unbiased extension of quantum-accelerated multilevel Monte Carlo (QA-MLMC) to eliminate all biases from discretization and time truncation, together with introducing a change-of-measure approach and the Girsanov theorem via Radon-Nikodym derivatives. As a result, our approach achieves quantum complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-1})$ within error $\epsilon$, whereas the classical MLMC requires $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2})$ and existing quantum algorithms yield biased estimators under stronger assumptions. Furthermore, our unified framework enables unbiased quantum sampling and estimation for certain heavy-tailed distributions after transformation. We provide several concrete applications of our approach in statistics, machine learning, and finance, towards more practical scenarios of the quantum acceleration of stochastic processes.
item.dc:creator: Xinmiao Li, Jin-Peng Liu

item.title: Scalable Determination of Penalization Weights for Constrained Optimizations on Approximate Solvers
item.description: arXiv:2604.02416v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) provides problem formulations for various computational problems that can be solved with dedicated QUBO solvers, based on classical or quantum computation. A common approach to constrained combinatorial optimization problems is to enforce the constraints in the QUBO formulation by adding penalization terms. Penalization introduces an additional hyperparameter that significantly affects the solver's efficacy: the relative weight between the objective terms and the penalization terms. Here we study the problem of a priori determining suitable penalization weights from a foundational and practical perspective. We formally establish that finding its optimal value for Gibbs solvers is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard even approximately and $\#\mathsf{P}$-hard exactly. This serves us as a motivation to develop a widely applicable heuristic strategy for determining suitable penalization weights, with provable guarantees for Gibbs solvers, and polynomial complexity for broad problem classes. Experiments across diverse problems and solver architectures, including large-scale instances on Fujitsu's Digital Annealer, show robust performance and order-of-magnitude speedups over existing heuristics. We further extend the strategy to quantum approximate optimization and demonstrate its performance on Quantinuum's H2-2 trapped-ion processor.
item.dc:creator: Edoardo Alessandroni, Sergi Ramos-Calderer, Michel Krispin, Markus Kirsch, Christian M\"unch, Fritz Schinkel, Stefan Walter, Martin Kliesch, Leandro Aolita, Ingo Roth

item.title: One pure steered state implies Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering for two-qubit entangled states
item.description: arXiv:2605.18243v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we show that a two-qubit entangled state admitting at least one pure steered state is Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) steerable from Alice to Bob. Pure steered states signifies that the quantum steering ellipsoid of Bob is tangent to his Bloch sphere at least at a single point. Furthermore, we prove that for a two-qubit entangled state, Bob's quantum steering ellipsoid is tangent to his Bloch sphere at exactly $N$ points, for $N\in \{ 0,1,2,\infty\}$, if and only if Alice's quantum steering ellipsoid is tangent to her Bloch sphere at exactly $N$ points. For any two-qubit entangled state, therefore, if one party can steer the other to at least one pure state, the state is two-way EPR steerable. We also present several illuminating examples of two-qubit entangled states such that the EPR steering can be verified in terms of pure steered states. Our result addresses the Gisin theorem in a EPR steering scenario: at least a single pure steered state implies two-way steering.
item.dc:creator: Qiu-Cheng Song, Joonwoo Bae

item.title: On Performance and Limitations of Quantum Wave Packet Dynamics Simulated using NISQ Hardware
item.description: arXiv:2605.20078v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate one-dimensional quantum wave-packet dynamics using a grid-based encoding of the wave function onto qubit registers. Time evolution is implemented using a split operator approach, with the kinetic energy operator realized via the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and arbitrary discretized potentials represented by commuting Pauli-Z gates. The algorithm is benchmarked against classical grid-based simulations and validated using a noiseless Qiskit Statevector simulator before being implemented on current quantum hardware (IBM Quantum and IonQ) for qubit counts ranging from two to five. Good agreement with benchmark calculations is obtained for two- and three-qubit implementations, while deviations increase at larger qubit counts due to hardware noise and increased circuit depth. Among the devices examined, the algorithm maintains closer agreement with the benchmark on the trapped-ion IonQ Forte processor as the number of qubits increases.
item.dc:creator: Tamila Kuanysheva, Jonathan Andrade-Plascencia, Jayakrushna Sahoo, Brian Kendrick, Dmitri Babikov

item.title: Geometric Construction of Optimal Teleportation Witnesses
item.description: arXiv:2605.22226v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Not all entangled states are useful for quantum teleportation. We present a geometric method to construct optimal teleportation witnesses, which provide operational necessary and sufficient criteria for identifying the teleportation usefulness of arbitrary two-qudit entangled states. Specifically, by developing a two-layer iterative cutting-plane algorithm to solve the shortest distance problem from the target state $\rho$ to the convex set $S$ of useless states, we obtain the projection point $\sigma^* \in S$ and then construct the optimal teleportation witness from the projection geometry. Moreover, the shortest distance $D(\rho)$ obtained during this construction also serves as a necessary and sufficient criterion for usefulness. We apply our method to identify the teleportation usefulness of three classes of entangled states.
item.dc:creator: Yanning Jia, Fenzhuo Guo, Mengxuan Bai, Mengyan Li, Haifeng Dong, Fei Gao

item.title: QML-PipeGuard: Detecting Channel-Substitution Attacks on Quantum Machine Learning Pipelines in Untrusted Clouds
item.description: arXiv:2605.25066v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As machine-learning workloads move onto quantum hardware they inherit a trust problem classical AI deployments have largely solved and quantum ones have not: quantum machine learning (QML) is already sold as a cloud service, and a customer cannot check that the circuit they paid for is actually the circuit that ran. We show the gap is exploitable. A malicious or cost-cutting provider can substitute the declared quantum channel with one that reproduces every accuracy test the customer performs, passes the single-observable checks used in practice, and still differs from the declared computation at the channel level. We call this a channel-substitution attack and instantiate it in three deployments: audit evasion, service downgrade, and result forgery in reproducibility review. QML-PipeGuard detects the attack at runtime from measurement statistics the customer already collects. Its guarantee is two-sided, stated in the distance a local verifier measures: any substitution shifting a single-qubit output marginal by $\delta$ in trace norm forces a contract deviation of at least $\delta/\sqrt{3}$, the constant tight and independent of qubit count; the guarantee is relative to the chosen observable family and reference-input set. For local-unitary substitutions the adversary's blind set is characterised exactly, as a commutation condition, which gives the defender a rule for choosing challenge inputs that shrinks it. A finite-shot budget rule bounds false accepts and false alarms at once, one tolerance separates attack from the benign drift observed here, and every decision enters a hash-anchored audit trail. On an IBM Heron r2 processor a substituted quantum-kernel intrusion-detection pipeline evades the weak contract and our verifier halts it, while the honest channel stays within tolerance.
item.dc:creator: Esra Yeniaras

item.title: Continuous-time quantum control across an exponentially small bottleneck in a frustrated Ising ring model
item.description: arXiv:2606.07168v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuous-time Quantum Annealing (QA) is a strategy for preparing the ground state of nontrivial many-body systems. In its standard form, the dynamics is generated by a time-dependent interpolation between a simple driving Hamiltonian and the target problem Hamiltonian, usually implemented through a linear schedule. This approach faces the crucial bottleneck of small spectral gaps, which may require exponentially long annealing times to ensure adiabaticity. Here, we show how to implement quantum control over the annealing schedule in a frustrated Ising ring, one of the simplest models exhibiting an exponentially small bottleneck gap. By optimizing smooth continuous-time annealing schedules with a dressed-CRAB approach, and using a digitized representation of the dynamics to efficiently evaluate gradients, we construct protocols that strongly outperform standard fixed schedules. The optimized dynamics bypasses the bottleneck through a strongly nonadiabatic mechanism, leading to efficient ground-state preparation despite the exponentially small minimum gap. In particular, the annealing time required to reach a fixed residual-energy threshold is found to grow linearly with system size rather than exponentially. We further examine a lowest-order variational counter-diabatic correction and find that, once schedule optimization is allowed, it does not lead to any improvement.
item.dc:creator: Vincenzo Roberto Arezzo, Kiran Thengil, Giuseppe Santoro

item.title: Complete Relational Description of Spin in a Quantum Background
item.description: arXiv:2606.15873v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The standard description of the state of a spin in quantum mechanics presupposes externally fixed directions -- a classical background. Can a spin be fully described instead in relation to other quantum mechanical systems? Poulin suggested twenty years ago group averaging over rotations the joint state of a fundamental spin and a reference spin with large angular momentum which, however, yields a classical bit in a probabilistic mixture. We revisit this idea and show that when the quantum reference system is augmented to \emph{two} large spins, the standard quantum mechanical description of a spin is recovered in the limit of large quantum numbers for the reference system.
item.dc:creator: Hannah Troger, Ofek Bengyat, Thomas D. Galley, Marios Christodoulou

item.title: Operator learning for efficient quantum computation
item.description: arXiv:2606.20184v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An efficient implementation of quantum algorithms is often hindered by the lack of efficient primitives for operators and state preparation. This limits both the ability of near-term quantum hardware to simulate complex problems and the potential of fault-tolerant algorithms to achieve practical quantum advantage. To address this, we propose a framework that maps discrete operators onto compact, structured quantum circuits. The resulting variational circuits can be tailored to the connectivity and long-range interaction of the target hardware. The learning process employs backpropagation together with a cost function that efficiently optimizes unitary operators and non-unitary --dense or sparse-- operators using only a single ancilla qubit for block encoding. Additionally, we introduce a regularization term that reduces the approximation error. The approach is validated for both quantum mechanical and engineering applications. In the former case, we learn propagators that arise in native quantum problems --such as quantum simulation and quantum chemistry-- and achieve improved resource scaling in comparison to standard Suzuki--Trotter expansions. In the latter case, we demonstrate the approach's ability to implement the second-order central finite difference approximation of the Laplace operator --relevant for solving partial differential equations-- while improving upon current error metrics. The final example deals with learning a dense, non-unitary operator that arises in the analysis of inviscid potential flow around an airfoil. These results motivate the extension of the framework to a broader class of operator-synthesis problems beyond the prototypical engineering and quantum applications considered here.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Quantum Science and Technology -- IOP Publishing Ltd -- October 2026
item.dc:creator: Paul Over, Sergio Bengoechea, Leonardo Borello Busilacchi, Martin Kiffner, Thomas Rung, Alexios A. Michailidis

item.title: Higher-Order Magnus Corrections to Leakage Elimination Operator-Based Quantum Control Pulse Design in the Low-Frequency Regime
item.description: arXiv:2606.29854v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Effective quantum control is essential for quantum computing and information processing, yet level leakage remains a bottleneck limiting control fidelity. The leakage elimination operator (LEO) approach is highly effective at suppressing leakage from a target subspace to other subspaces. Analytical control conditions under the high-frequency driving limit have been derived via the Feshbach PQ partitioning technique. However, the driving intensity is subject to fundamental physical bounds, and low-frequency driving is experimentally more feasible. In this work, we reformulate LEO within the Magnus framework and extend it beyond the high-frequency limit. We show that the analytical control conditions obtained from the Feshbach PQ partitioning technique are equivalent to the zeroth-order Magnus expansion. We then analyze the higher-order Magnus corrections. By minimizing the leakage, we obtain a modified pulse condition suitable for the low-frequency regime. As an illustrative example, we study near-perfect state transfer through a one-dimensional spin chain under LEO control. We find that the second-order Magnus correction improves the transmission fidelity at low-frequency driving, while the improvement becomes negligible at high frequencies. Our results provide an effective route for designing control pulses in the low-frequency regime, with potential applications in superconducting qubits, trapped ions, and solid-state spin systems.
item.dc:creator: Hang Yu, Kai-Yu Yuan, Feng-Hua Ren, Zhao-Ming Wang

item.title: Cooperative control of dissipative qubits: steering along the fastest dissipative contraction
item.description: arXiv:2606.30073v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the control of dissipative quantum systems, the slow relaxation modes usually set the ultimate manipulation timescale. We show that this bottleneck can be bypassed when dissipation itself is used as the engine of the transfer. For a qubit with non-unital, anisotropic Bloch relaxation characterized by the ratio $\kappa=T_1/T_2>1$, coherent control can only rotate the Bloch vector, whereas the bath alone can change its length. The fastest transfer between two thermal states therefore consists in steering the Bloch vector, at every instant, along the direction in which the bath contracts it most rapidly. This direction is obtained in closed form and lies slightly beyond the equatorial plane. With strong pulses, the resulting minimum transfer time is a fraction of $T_2$, instead of several $T_1$ for passive relaxation. With bounded fields, the Pontryagin maximum principle yields a bang--singular--bang synthesis whose singular arc is precisely this fastest-contraction direction, and the minimum time exceeds its strong-pulse limit by a correction inversely proportional to the field amplitude. We also determine the full time--energy Pareto front: moderate accelerations require little energy, and the time optimum lies at its steep, high-energy end. Off-axis targets are treated within the same framework; their only additional benefit is a shorter final rotation. These results apply directly to magnetic-resonance spins, nitrogen-vacancy centers and superconducting qubits, all of which operate deep in the strong-pulse regime.
item.dc:creator: Robert Wei{\ss}, Sandro Wimberger, David Gu\'ery-Odelin

item.title: Time-Reversal and Reversible Dynamics in Cavity QED for Quantum Metrology
item.description: arXiv:2607.02320v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum-enhanced metrology relies on entanglement to achieve sensitivities beyond the standard quantum limit. While remarkable progress has been made in generating highly entangled many-body states, extracting their metrological advantage remains a central challenge because the encoded information is often inaccessible to realistic measurements. A key development of the past decade has been the realization that many-body interactions can play a dual role: they can be used not only to generate entanglement, but also to decode it. This idea underlies interaction-based readout and time-reversal protocols, in which controlled non-linear dynamics transform weakly encoded signals into experimentally accessible observables. Cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED) provides a particularly powerful setting for these approaches because it combines collective enhancement, tunable interactions, and controllable reversibility within a single platform. In this review, we discuss the emergence of time-reversal protocols in cavity QED, from their conceptual roots in Loschmidt echoes to modern implementations of signal amplification through a time-reversed interaction (SATIN), scrambling-enhanced metrology, and more general interaction-based readout schemes. We examine the physical mechanisms that enable reversible many-body dynamics, review key experimental demonstrations, and discuss future directions involving complex entangled states, nonlinear decoding, and emerging quantum platforms. Together, these developments suggest that the ability to decode quantum information may become as important as the ability to generate it, establishing reversible many-body dynamics as a central resource for quantum-enhanced sensing.
item.dc:creator: Simone Colombo, Edwin Pedrozo-Pe\~nafiel

item.title: Temperature Beyond Equilibrium in Isolated Quantum Many-Body Systems and Their Subsystems
item.description: arXiv:2607.08655v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Temperature is one of the central concepts of thermodynamics, yet its meaning far from equilibrium remains unclear. The problem is especially challenging in isolated quantum many-body systems, whose states evolve unitarily, may remain far from equilibrium, and retain energy coherence, a genuinely quantum feature with no direct classical counterpart. Specifically, energy fluctuations in a nonstationary quantum state have two distinct origins. Part of these fluctuations comes from uncertainty in the energy populations and has the usual thermodynamic meaning. The rest comes from quantum coherence between energy sectors and is responsible for the state's time dependence. We propose that, even away from equilibrium, temperature identifies the state within the family of regular states sharing the same energy-coherence structure. The resulting inverse temperature is obtained from a principle of minimum discrimination information, which selects the least distinguishable state compatible with the prescribed energy and coherence structure. This replaces the usual maximum-entropy principle, which, applied naively, can yield a biased estimator of the inverse temperature. We also lay the groundwork for an extension of the construction to subsystems and show that, although the inverse temperature of a subsystem is not determined by its reduced state alone, under an alignment assumption, its instantaneous rate of change is a local quantity for sufficiently large subsystems.
item.dc:creator: Maurizio Fagotti

item.title: Classical probabilistic realisation of quantum double-slit interference
item.description: arXiv:2607.11580v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We demonstrate how the interference effects for a quantum particle in the double-slit experiment can be described by classical probabilities. We investigate a classical field theory for a complex scalar field with probabilistic initial conditions. A central element are conserved charges leading to the concept of particles. These are statistical observables which describe properties of the probability distribution for field configurations. The conserved charges define subsystems for particle excitations of a vacuum state. The classical probability distribution for the one-particle subsystem can be expressed in terms of a complex wave function. The Liouville equation for the classical probability distribution implies that the time evolution of this wave function obeys the Schr\"odinger equation for a quantum particle in a potential. The potential arises from space-dependent external fields in the otherwise relativistic classical field theory. It can be chosen arbitrarily, realizing the typical quantum effects of interference, tunneling or discrete energy spectra.
item.dc:creator: Christof Wetterich

item.title: Proof-of-Principle Implementation of Quantum Key Distribution in an Indefinite Causal Order
item.description: arXiv:2608.13561v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In quantum physics, the order in which different operations occur can be placed in superposition. The resulting processes have an indefinite causal order, which is of fundamental interest and can be viewed as a novel quantum resource enabling new protocols. Here, we report an experimental proof-of-principle implementation of one such protocol, where we perform BB84-like quantum cryptography by placing \AB's measurement-and-preparation operations in a photonic quantum SWITCH. By embedding \AB\ within the quantum SWITCH, the protocol achieves an average eavesdropper detection probability of $0.15 \pm 0.02$ per shared qubit, with eavesdropper detection performed through measurements of the control qubit rather than comparing the key. Unlike standard BB84 and related schemes, which detect eavesdropping by publicly revealing and discarding a fraction of the raw key, our approach requires no disclosure of key material: every retained qubit can, in principle, be tested for eavesdropping while remaining available for key generation. Although the present implementation does not yet constitute a secure quantum key distribution protocol, owing to post-selection required for measurements within the quantum SWITCH, it provides a proof of principle that indefinite causal order can be exploited to detect eavesdropping without sacrificing key bits.
item.dc:creator: Yann Valibouse, Mart\'i Cladera-Rossell\'o, Michael Antesberger, Hector Spencer-Wood, Kyrylo Simonov, Patrik Sund, Mathieu Bozzio, Philip Walther, Lee A. Rozema

item.title: Parallel Quantum Advantage with Limited Adaptivity Requires Structure
item.description: arXiv:2608.20297v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Aaronson and Ambainis (Theory of Computing, 2014) conjectured that quantum query algorithms admit efficient almost-everywhere classical simulation: for any $T$-query quantum algorithm, its acceptance probability can be approximated on a $(1-\delta)$ fraction of inputs, up to $\epsilon$ additive error, using $\mathrm{poly}(T, 1/\epsilon, 1/\delta)$ classical queries. At a high level, the conjecture suggests that exponential quantum speedups are possible only on sufficiently structured inputs. In this work, we make progress on this conjecture by proving it for quantum algorithms that make massively parallel quantum queries. In contrast, Yamakawa and Zhandry (Journal of the ACM, 2024) showed that quantum algorithms restricted to parallel queries can still achieve exponential speedups over classical algorithms for sampling problems. We establish our simulation theorem by proving the stronger statement that parallel-query quantum algorithms cannot distinguish the uniform distribution over oracles from oracles drawn from so-called "dense distributions". Our main technical contribution is a coupling theorem that relates the uniform distribution over oracles to oracles drawn from dense distributions. We further extend this approach beyond the purely parallel setting. We prove simulation theorems for quantum algorithms with constant rounds of adaptivity, and for quantum algorithms with a bounded quantum-query prefix followed by a massively parallel quantum-query stage.
item.dc:creator: Qipeng Liu, Saachi Mutreja

item.title: Taming Spacetime Overhead and Design Complexity in Distributed Fault-Tolerant Superconducting Quantum Computation
item.description: arXiv:2608.23159v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers will likely require distributed architectures built from multiple manufacturable quantum processing units. A central question is whether noisy and slow inter-chip operations impose substantial spacetime overhead or orchestration burdens compared with monolithic architectures. To answer this question, we present a hardware-grounded architectural co-design together with a comprehensive resource-estimation protocol for surface-code-based modular processors. The design confines inter-chip latency and noise to module boundaries, preventing slow, noisy links from inducing prohibitive spacetime overhead or becoming a global orchestration bottleneck. The resource-estimation protocol integrates hardware constraints and circuit-level error-correction performance into utility-scale algorithmic cost estimates, enabling a controlled assessment of different architectures. Using RSA-2048 factorization as a demanding benchmark, we estimate resources under experimentally anchored parameters and realistic superconducting hardware constraints. Compared with a large, ideal monolithic baseline, the resulting distributed architecture requires only modest additional resource overhead in both qubit count and execution time. More importantly, the overhead is nearly scale-invariant across a broad module-capacity window, decoupling chip size from global performance. This decoupling turns module capacity from a finely tuned architectural parameter into a flexible engineering degree of freedom, allowing chip sizes to be set by manufacturability and control-packaging constraints rather than architectural fine-tuning. These results establish a viable route to distributed fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computation that scales without prohibitive resource growth or heavy orchestration burden.
item.dc:creator: Qinjing Yu, Ke Liu

item.title: Wigner Time: from experimental intent to real-time laboratory control
item.description: arXiv:2609.06230v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Precisely timed, multi-device control in atomic, molecular and optical physics is provided by specialized real-time systems, which impose their own terms on the description of the experiment: a program over a global clock, in which every stage boundary is an absolute time computed from everything preceding it. Such descriptions are tightly coupled -- changing one stage affects all later ones -- and are correspondingly hard to reuse, inspect, or move elsewhere. We introduce Wigner Time, a Python package in which the experimental procedure is instead represented as data: a table of timed updates, assembled by composing functions and referred to named points in the experiment rather than to absolute instants. Hardware enters only at a final conversion step, leaving the description readable and back-end agnostic. Wigner Time has run two cold-atom setups for more than two years, where taking the computation out of the real-time program improved the achievable temporal resolution five-fold; the design applies to any domain requiring precise multi-device timing.
item.dc:creator: T. W. Clark, B. S\'ark\"ozi, A. Dombi, \'A. Kurk\'o, D. Nagy, A. Simon, D. Varga, P. Domokos, A. Vukics

item.title: Propaq: A Python package for Heisenberg Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2609.07730v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Propaq, a performant and flexible Python package implementing Heisenberg propagation techniques for classically simulating quantum circuits. Propaq is compatible with major quantum software packages like Qiskit and Cirq, and matches or outperforms similar state-of-the-art packages for Heisenberg propagation. Beyond this, Propaq has multiple distinguishing features for simulation and research. These include Heisenberg propagation in any basis, hybrid Schr\"{o}dinger-Heisenberg simulation, custom truncation and noisy simulation methods, and detailed logging information for analyzing simulation accuracy, runtime, and memory usage. We describe these features, how to use Propaq for research, and its backend implementation.
item.dc:creator: Hrishikesh Belagali, Ryan LaRose

item.title: The Low-Individual-Degree Test Without the Diagonal-Lines Test Is Not Quantum-Sound
item.description: arXiv:2609.12346v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To prove the quantum soundness of the classical low-individual-degree test, the authors of \cite{JNVWY20LID} defined three subtests, namely the axis-parallel lines test, the self-consistency test, and the diagonal-lines test. An interesting question is whether the diagonal-lines test can be removed. In this paper, we show that the diagonal-lines test cannot simply be removed without another compatibility mechanism. Consequently, replacing the "conditional linear functions" by "coordinate deletion functions" in the proof of MIP*=RE, as mentioned in \cite{JNVWY20LID}, does not by itself preserve the required soundness. The authors of \cite{JNVWY20LID} found an example that requires the diagonal-lines test when \((m, d, q) = (2, 2, 4)\); we give an example when \((m, d) = (2, 2)\) and \(q\) is any odd prime.
item.dc:creator: Honghao Fu, Nengkun Yu, Tianrun Zhao

item.title: Local Optimality Does Not Compose: Invariant Simplices and the Complexity of Shared Probabilistic Automata
item.description: arXiv:2609.19707v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Probabilistic models are often constructed separately for different test suites and then expected to share a single latent dynamical system. We study bounded-state shared realization for probabilistic automata from finite partial trace specifications. A shared realization uses one normalized automaton with named initial distributions, a common family of row-stochastic letter-transition matrices, and one final output vector. We compare it with separate local realizations and a labelled query-specific static relaxation. Local and labelled query-specific static optima need not compose. For every $k,L\ge1$, we construct finite partial specifications for which each individual specification and the labelled query-specific static relaxation have minimum state count $k$, whereas every exact shared realization requires exactly $k(L+1)$ states. The factor $L+1$ reflects the prefix progress that must be tracked by a single shared transition family. In the linear-rank-tight calibrated regime, the existence of an exact $k$-state shared realization is equivalent to finding a $(k-1)$-simplex containing the root responses, contained in the response polytope, and forward-invariant under every single-letter affine update. For finite rational specifications, exact shared realization with at most $K$ states is $\exists\mathbb{R}$-complete, while distinguishing zero minimax defect from inverse-polynomial defect is $\mathsf{PromiseNP}$-complete. Both classifications hold over a fixed five-letter alphabet when the local and labelled query-specific static optima already equal $K$. They remain valid with Boolean final output vectors, and the robust gap persists over the full cube $[0,1]^d$. Thus the hardness arises from shared word composition.
item.dc:creator: Yixin Zhao

item.title: Observable-targeted variational quantum simulation of Hamiltonian dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2609.24794v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Standard variational quantum simulation seeks to reproduce the evolution of the full quantum state, although many applications require only the expectation values of a few observables. We study a variational method for pure-state Hamiltonian dynamics that updates circuit parameters to reproduce the evolution of selected expectation values. An exact error identity guides the choice of observables, motivating a construction based on repeated commutators of the target with the Hamiltonian. For Pauli observables and Pauli-rotation circuits, the update can be estimated without ancillary qubits or controlled operations for overlap estimation. Across six- and ten-qubit spin, fermionic, and molecular benchmarks, the observable-targeted update extends the median time within the target-error tolerance compared with standard variational quantum simulation with equal shot budgets. These results show that directing the variational update toward the target observable can extend accurate simulation without increasing the measurement cost per time step.
item.dc:creator: Leonardo Zambrano, Luciano Pereira, Antonio Ac\'in

item.title: Quantum Soundness of a Total-Degree Line-versus-Point Test
item.description: arXiv:2609.27129v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove quantum soundness of the total-degree diagonal line-vs-point test using the individual-degree soundness theorem of Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, and Yuen. A random change of coordinates yields projective polynomial decoders of total degree at most $md$. The uniform-line slice of the test bounds the weight of outcomes of degree greater than $d$, which are removed by a common relabeling. This reduction does not yield a dimension-independent soundness bound: the $\operatorname{poly}(m)$ dependence of the individual-degree theorem persists, as discussed in Section 1.2 of arXiv:2009.12982.
item.dc:creator: Honghao Fu, Nengkun Yu, Tianrun Zhao

item.title: Angular momentum conservation in two-atom superradiance
item.description: arXiv:2609.31433v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Two-atom superradiance is studied for atoms having a J=0 ground state and a J=1 excited state. The atoms lie on the x-axis and are excited by a \sigma_{+}-polarized laser pulse propagating in the z-direction. We use two, complementary approaches to obtain the final angular momentum in the field, a source-field approach and a Schrodinger picture approach. Both approaches give identical answers, but it is necessary to include terms in both calculations that, at first glance, might not be expected to contribute. We show that, owing to an exchange between a state in which atom 1 is in its m=1 excited state and atom 2 is in its ground state to one in which atom 2 is in its m=-1 excited state and atom 1 in its ground state, the final angular momentum in the field is not necessarily equal to the initial angular momentum in the two-atom system. The missing angular momentum appears as orbital angular momentum of the two atoms.
item.dc:creator: P. R. Berman, Zeyuan Wang, A. Kuzmich

item.title: Near-Optimal Quantum Algorithm and Complexity Analysis for Riccati Problems
item.description: arXiv:2609.37207v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop quantum algorithms that construct block-encodings of solution matrices for continuous- and discrete-time algebraic Riccati equations (CAREs and DAREs), differential Riccati equations (DREs), and finite Riccati recursions. The Quantum Weighted Riesz Method, unifying four kinds of Riccati problems, constructs projectors onto the solution graphs using weighted Riesz branching operators and recovers the solution matrices. Under the stated access and normalization assumptions, our algorithms for CAREs and DAREs have near-optimal query complexity $\Theta(\mathcal R\alpha)$ up to logarithmic factors, with the generalized singularity factor $\mathcal R$ that reflects spectral separation, and the output normalization $\alpha$. For DREs and finite-horizon problems, the query complexity has an additional initialization conditioning factor $\kappa_{\rm init}$. We establish product query lower bounds for specified input-oracle families, demonstrating necessary joint dependence on spectral separation and initialization or output scale. We also prove that selected-value promise problems are BQP-complete on explicit circuit-generated families of single-control discrete-time algebraic and zero-terminal differential Riccati equations. Applications include classical feedback evaluation for linear-quadratic control, a query-complexity comparison for stable random-phase approximation Riccati equations in quantum chemistry, and heated boundary control with numerical validation.
item.dc:creator: Jingyao Wang, Yanqiao Wang, Bowen Li, Jin-Peng Liu, Zhengfeng Ji

item.title: Gap-Protected Heisenberg-Limited Squeezing with Locally Interacting Multi-Level Spins
item.description: arXiv:2610.02314v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We demonstrate a general mechanism to generate scalable, metrologically useful entanglement in the form of generalized spin squeezing in multi-level (qudit) spin systems with power-law interactions. We demonstrate this for spin-changing dynamics, extending the physics of spin-nematic squeezing known from spinor BECs to spatially extended lattice geometries. In the absence of all-to-all connectivity, the dynamics generally suffers from leakage into non-collective finite-momentum modes, destroying Heisenberg scaling. We show that introducing local $\mathfrak{su}(D)$ exchange interactions establishes an energy gap that protects the fully symmetric collective manifold, suppressing non-collective excitations, and achieving Heisenberg scaling $\xi^2\propto1/N$ in one to three dimensions for any power-law exponent. We provide an analytical understanding of the mechanism via the analysis of the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum, and demonstrate its effectiveness via numerical simulations of the quantum many-body dynamics. Our findings more broadly apply to other spin-squeezing Hamiltonians, and directly generalize to larger internal spin dimensions. Our results provide a practical pathway towards scalable Heisenberg-limited qudit entanglement generation in experimental platforms such as arrays of (polar) molecules, magnetic atoms, and Rydberg atoms realizing multi-level spin systems.
item.dc:creator: Sakshi Bahamnia, Sagar Chaudhary, Arman Duha, Thomas Bilitewski

item.title: Classical Verification of a Remote Quantum Processor via Degenerate Concordant Computations: An Application to Randomness Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.08185v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A client renting a cloud quantum processor cannot easily tell whether its bitstrings came from a quantum device. Certification by random circuit sampling runs on present hardware, but scoring each sample costs $O(2^n)$. We give a protocol in which the client scores each round in $O(n)$ time, based on degenerate concordant ensembles: mixed states that are classical probability distributions over a product basis, with several basis states sharing a probability. For such a state, every concordance-preserving gate factorizes into local basis changes, a relabeling of basis states, and a block factor rotating labels of equal probability. This factor commutes with the state, so it cancels from the ensemble while entangling each pure component. The client holds a secret parity whose cosets are the degenerate sectors of every layer, enabling circuit construction and ensemble prediction with one inner product per layer. The secret never leaves the client. Uniformly random inputs are sent, and the client privately records each input's eigenvalue in the hidden state. An input--output agreement test and a weighted collision test compare server samples with the computation's non-flat output distribution. We prove completeness, client efficiency, and soundness in an ideal model where the compiled circuit reveals nothing about the secret; a classical server holding it passes. For the explicit construction, we prove that the single-qubit symmetry test used in efficient concordant-computation simulations fails on non-product inputs with unbiased marginals. We also find that a published local-basis finder halts on every tested layer, the transmitted component attains maximal Schmidt rank, the circuit is non-Clifford, and matrix-product spoofers are rejected. Soundness of the explicit construction remains conjectural.
item.dc:creator: Bishal Kumar Das, Lakshya Priyadarshi

item.title: Pauli Decomposition by Character Theory: A Memory-Bounded Algorithm for Qubits and Qudits
item.description: arXiv:2610.08299v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pauli decomposition of an $n$-qubit operator is expensive if each of the $4^n$ Pauli strings is treated as an unstructured object. Labeling those strings by the configuration space $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^n$ makes them displacement operators $X^{\otimes x}Z^{\otimes z}$ on the computational space: shifts by~$x$ and multiplications by characters $Z^{\otimes z}$ in the computational basis. That labeling organizes the operator into $2^n$ fibers of length $2^n$, one per shift~$x$, each collecting the computational-basis amplitudes that hop by~$x$. Expanding each fiber function in the character basis of $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^n$ --- a length-$2^n$ Walsh--Hadamard transform --- recovers the Pauli coefficients at total cost $O(n\cdot4^n)$. The same fiber / shift--character picture extends to $(\mathbb{Z}_p)^n$ (Heisenberg--Weyl qudits). \texttt{paulikit} is a memory-bounded realization for qubits: for matrix-sparse inputs, peak memory need not densify to a full $2^n\times2^n$ operator. Performance is checked on a stated low-end GNU/Linux platform for a coupled-oscillator sweep beyond a billion Pauli terms.
item.dc:creator: Mohammadreza Khellat, Mohammad Masoumi, Saman Nasoori, Soroush Nasoori

item.title: The surprising simplicity of forecasting quantum chaotic many-body dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.10697v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurately simulating chaotic quantum many-body dynamics remains a major computational challenge for classical methods, due to the rapid buildup and spatial spreading of entanglement during the evolution. This raises the question of whether machine learning can provide an effective alternative for predicting quantum dynamics. We address this question by formulating quantum dynamics as a time-series forecasting problem, using a few-qubit PXP chain, realizable with Rydberg-atom arrays, as a benchmark. By varying the initial state, the system spans dynamical regimes ranging from ergodic behavior to quantum many-body scarring, providing a controlled setting for testing forecasting models across qualitatively different dynamics. We compare two contrasting architectures: an expressive nonlinear Transformer and DLinear, a simple linear forecasting model. The Transformer accurately predicts dynamics in the more ergodic regime, but its performance progressively deteriorates as the initial state approaches the scarred limit. In contrast, DLinear remains accurate across the entire family of initial states, with its main deviations consisting of small high-frequency oscillations that have little effect on the overall prediction error. Remarkably, these results show that observables generated by complex quantum many-body dynamics can be forecast with high accuracy through a simple linear mapping from past to future observations. This reveals that the complexity of the underlying quantum evolution need not translate into an equally complex forecasting problem.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Perciavalle, Agostino Gallo, Francesco Plastina, Gianluigi Greco, Nicola Lo Gullo, Carlo Adornetto

item.title: Riemannian Formulation of Sample-Based Quantum Krylov Solvers for Elliptic Problems: Energy-Norm Guarantees and Duct-Flow Applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.15586v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sample-based quantum linear solvers measure quantum Krylov states $e^{-iAT}|b\rangle$ and reconstruct the solution of $Ax=b$ classically on the observed basis states. We develop this approach for positive-definite systems that arise from elliptic partial differential equations. We show that the sampling guarantees hold in any fixed basis with an efficient transform. We then replace the variational reconstruction by a Galerkin solve on the sampled set. For this reconstruction we derive expected and high-probability energy-norm error bounds, a sample complexity in terms of the smallest sampling probability on an essential set, a computable residual certificate, and a support-completeness theorem for the dephased outcome law. We formulate the method for elliptic problems on Riemannian cross sections. In two dimensions the stiffness matrix is metric-independent in conformal coordinates, and curved vessels lead to the same matrix class. Killing symmetries of the cross section give selection rules for the measurement outcomes, and the Lie derivative of the metric gives first-order bounds for geometric perturbations. We separate operator approximations, whose effect we bound, from sampler approximations, which affect coverage but not the target. As examples we treat the implicit step of pulsatile flow in elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts. In simulations of up to 12 qubits, the number of Fourier modes required for 1% error grows from 14 to 60 while the number of unknowns grows from 64 to 4096. A classical residual-greedy selection is nevertheless more efficient than quantum sampling in all cases studied, consistent with the low measured sampling efficiency. On a six-qubit trapped-ion processor, the measured outcome laws follow a replacement-noise model whose strength grows by about 0.6% per two-qubit gate, and a parity selection rule rejects shots at the predicted rate.
item.dc:creator: Doyeol "David" Ahn (Center for Quantum Information Processing, University of Seoul, Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul, Republic of Korea, Singularity Quantum Inc., Villa Park, California, USA), Byeongyong Park (Center for Quantum Information Processing, University of Seoul, Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul, Republic of Korea)

item.title: PPVM: A Circuit Simulation Framework for Digital Twins of Quantum Processors
item.description: arXiv:2610.18225v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum computers are approaching the early fault-tolerant regime. Verifying the next generation of quantum hardware requires joint emulation of the quantum processor, hardware noise, and classical control and decoding logic. We introduce the Programmable Pauli Virtual Machine (PPVM), an open-source framework for digital twins of quantum processors. PPVM unifies Pauli propagation and generalized tableau simulation under a common abstraction within a single virtual machine. Its bytecode supports arbitrary classical control flow, with measurement-conditioned feed-forward available in the generalized tableau backend. For neutral-atom hardware, we derive independent and correlated atom-loss channels and integrate them into both backends. We demonstrate loss-aware magic state distillation on over a thousand physical qubits and integration with classical decoding through Bloqade QEC Studio.
item.dc:creator: Xiu-Zhe Luo, David Plankensteiner, Kai-Hsin Wu, Rob Patterson, Alexander Schuckert, Oriol Rubies-Bigorda, Refaat Ismail, Jonhas Colina, Neelay Fruitwala, Danylo Lykov, Tyson Jones, Stefan Krastanov, Rafael Haenel, Stefan Ostermann, Sheng-Tao Wang

item.title: Scalable Tomography of Coherent Noise via Stabilizer-Code Polarization
item.description: arXiv:2610.19779v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coherent errors accumulate linearly rather than diffusively, making them invisible to Pauli-twirl-based char- acterization. It poses a central challenge for quantum error correction, yet its characterization typically requires multi-qubit process tomography whose cost grows exponentially with system size. We show that measurement- free error correction projects arbitrary few-qubit coherent noise onto a fixed single-logical-qubit effective chan- nel, enabling tomography at constant cost. Exploiting the polarization effects of bit-flip and phase-flip codes, we construct a concatenated effective-channel fingerprint and prove, by a parity-based contradiction argument, that the observation map is globally injective over a prescribed coherent-noise family; hence the underlying noise parameters are uniquely recovered without any sparsity or low-rank assumptions. The recovered coherent noise model can be fed into decoding algorithms; relative to independent noise priors, we expect this to reduce the logical error rate for surface-code decoders. The protocol offers a scalable route to coherent-noise identification whenever the noise admits a moderate-dimensional parameterization.
item.dc:creator: Long Huang

item.title: Majorana Edge Modes Reshape Kibble-Zurek Scaling in Kitaev Honeycomb Ribbons
item.description: arXiv:2610.19923v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent progress in programmable quantum simulators motivates exact benchmarks for nonequilibrium dynamics in topological quantum matter. We study the Kitaev honeycomb model driven through its critical regions by a linear ramp of the bond coupling $J_z$ over a ramp time $\tau$, comparing zigzag and armchair ribbons with fully periodic tubes. The production of excitations exhibits a geometry-dependent finite-size crossover controlled by $N_2/\sqrt{\tau}$, the ratio of the ribbon width to the Kibble--Zurek length. Periodic tubes obey the expected critical-line Kibble--Zurek scaling and serve as the boundary-free benchmark. Zigzag ribbons follow the same scaling until defect production is exponentially suppressed by a finite-width algebraic gap floor associated with the formation of Majorana edge modes, whose occupation is pinned by inversion parity. Armchair ribbons instead support transient Majorana edge modes with exponentially small gaps, producing width-parity-dependent defect plateaus: exactly one defect per unit length for odd widths and an approximate, transient plateau near one half for even widths. The quench-generated entanglement entropy and fermionic logarithmic negativity inherit the same geometry-dependent structure, and the negativity further distinguishes the coherence-borne entanglement of the Kibble--Zurek regime from the population-borne entanglement of the edge-mode plateaus. These results identify boundary Majorana modes as the mechanism controlling departures from ideal Kibble--Zurek dynamics and provide geometry-resolved benchmarks for programmable simulations of topological matter.
item.dc:creator: Hyesung Choi, Antonio Mandarino, Mahn-Soo Choi

item.title: Local finite rate semi device independent randomness expansion from quantum contextuality
item.description: arXiv:2610.21765v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Finite rate randomness expansion (RE) which is secure against quantum adversaries is a crucial information processing task which is well studied in the case of two non-communicating parties sharing Bell non-local correlations in a device independent manner. In this paper we show that contextual correlations with only a single localized party are sufficient for RE in a semi-device independent (SDI) manner. We propose a template SDI-RE protocol which is applicable for arbitrary $N$-cycle non-contextuality (NC) inequalities and derive its RE rate under finite statistics. As a special case, we also highlight the advantages of the situation when RE is constrained by Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality but with characterized measurements implemented by only a single party. Our template protocol also incorporates non-ideal statistics which may not satisfy perfect commutativity and perfect repeatability, both of which are necessary in a loophole-free test of NC inequalities. As such, several recent experimental implementations of significantly loophole-free tests of NC inequalities can be modified for secure RE following our approach.
item.dc:creator: Dhananjoy Ghosh, Nandana J, Jaskaran Singh

item.title: Quantum-Classical Iterative Refinement for the Pressure-Poisson Equation on NISQ Hardware
item.description: arXiv:2610.24342v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a hybrid quantum-classical iterative refinement for the pressure-Poisson equation of the incompressible Navier-Stokes projection method on noisy quantum hardware. Rather than solving the pressure equation once per time step, we solve it repeatedly for the normalized residual and scale each quantum direction by a least-squares fit to the physical residual. As a result, the error of the quantum solve enters as a contraction factor $\sin\theta_k$ of the residual rather than as an error floor. This removes the requirement of a state infidelity below $10^{-7}$ that was estimated for single-solve schemes. The hardware noise then sets the rate of convergence but not the attainable accuracy, and it is this change of the role of the quantum solve, not an improvement of the hardware, that allows the residual to converge. With a boundary-consistent staggered (MAC) discretization, the pressure residual equals the velocity divergence left after projection up to the factor $\Delta t/\rho$. On the IBM processor ibm_cleveland, a four-qubit ($16\times16$) problem reached a relative residual below $10^{-7}$ within eight to ten corrections in all 20 runs of a pre-registered experiment, whereas a single solve with a comparable number of shots stopped at 0.33-0.59. In a six-qubit ($64\times64$) pilot, all three runs reached the same tolerance in 13 corrections. On the IonQ Forte processor, a manufactured-solution benchmark reached $5.6\times10^{-8}$ in nine corrections. With the variational training itself carried out on ibm_cleveland, the residual fell to $5.6\times10^{-4}$ in seven corrections, below the pre-specified tolerance of $10^{-3}$, at the rate predicted by a noise model. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first converged pressure solutions obtained on quantum hardware.
item.dc:creator: Doyeol "David" Ahn (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Seoul, Seoul, Republic of Korea 2 Singularity Quantum Inc., Newport Beach, CA, USA 3 Center for Quantum Information Processing, University of Seoul, Seoul, Republic of Korea 4 School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Gyeongsang National University, Jinju, Republic of Korea 5 National Quantum Laboratory at Maryland), Byeongyong Park, Rho Shin Myong, Franz Klein

item.title: Theoretical Description of Electronic Modulation and Superconducting Coherence
item.description: arXiv:2512.03368v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An electronic modulation can retain a substantial local amplitude while its translational coherence is limited by spatial disorder. Its coupling to superconductivity therefore cannot be characterized by a single modulation intensity. We develop a phenomenological formulation of a finite-wave-vector complex electronic envelope coupled to a charged superconducting field. Translation and gauge symmetries constrain the interaction terms, while amplitude, modulation-gradient and condensate-gradient couplings act on distinct responses. The resulting variational equations give uniform coexistence conditions, local stability criteria and phase-gradient coefficients. We define the helicity modulus by a boundary twist, distinguish phase-only from amplitude-weighted correlations, and give an explicit minimal spectral Hamiltonian illustrating how the electronic texture may enter momentum-resolved measurements. The proposed tests use distinct spatial, spectral and stiffness observables; none assumes that a tunnelling gap directly measures condensate amplitude. An explicit kernel expansion yields the leading displacement of the selected wave vector, while the thermodynamic twist response determines phase rigidity independently of charge intensity. The analytical relations and selected numerical responses distinguish amplitude, spatial organization and condensate rigidity within the specified coupled-field model.
item.dc:creator: Jaehwahn Kim, Davis A. Rens, Waqas Khalid, Hyunchul Kim

item.title: The JLMS formula in a large code with approximate error correction
item.description: arXiv:2601.00442v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gauge/gravity duality is often described as a quantum error correcting code. However, as seen in the Jafferis-Lewkowycz-Maldacena-Suh (JLMS) formula, exact quantum error correction with complementary recovery (and thus entanglement wedge reconstruction) emerges only in the limit $G \to 0$. As a result, precise arguments controlling error terms have focused on what we call `small' codes which, as $G \to 0$, describe only perturbative excitations near a given classical solution. Such settings are quite restrictive and, in particular, they prohibit discussion of any modular flow that would change the classical background. As a result, they forbid consideration of modular flows generated by semiclassical bulk states at order-one modular parameters. In contrast, we present a single `large' code for the bulk theory that can accommodate such flows and, in particular, in the $G \to 0$ limit includes superpositions of states associated with distinct classical backgrounds. This large code is assembled from small codes that each satisfy an approximate Faulkner-Lewkowycz-Maldacena formula. In this extended setting we clarify the meaning of the (approximate) JLMS relation between bulk and boundary modular Hamiltonians and quantify its validity in an appropriate class of states.
item.dc:creator: Xi Dong, Donald Marolf, Pratik Rath

item.title: On the structural properties of Lie algebras via associated labeled directed graphs
item.description: arXiv:2601.16161v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a method for associating labeled directed graphs to finite-dimensional Lie algebras that are $graph$-$admissible$. The proposed framework enables visual identification of key structural algebraic features. We first formalize this approach and establish several classes of Lie algebras that admit the categorization as graph-admissible Lie algebras, and then investigate suitable valid graphs for this approach by translating the antisymmetry of the Lie bracket and the Jacobi identity into rules that such graphs must satisfy. Furthermore, based on these foundations, we provide graph-theoretic criteria for solvability, nilpotency, presence of ideals, simplicity, semisimplicity, and reductiveness of an algebra. We also present practical algorithms for constructing such graphs and those associated with the lower central series and derived series via iterative pruning procedures. We further cover specific examples, such as the Schr\"odinger and Lorentz algebras, which illustrate the applicability of the developed tools to physically relevant cases. Moreover, we explore applications in physics, where the method facilitates computation of similarity transformations essential for determining quantum mechanical time evolution via the Lie-algebraic factorization method. We also discuss a possible generalization of the framework based on magma-gradings of Lie algebras and formulate related open questions. Our approach bridges algebraic and combinatorial perspectives, offering theoretical tools for this area of mathematical physics.
item.dc:creator: Tim Heib, David Edward Bruschi

item.title: Graph-Theoretic Analysis of Phase Optimization Complexity in Variational Wave Functions for Heisenberg Antiferromagnets
item.description: arXiv:2602.04943v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the computational complexity of learning the ground state phase structure of Heisenberg antiferromagnets. Representing Hilbert space as a weighted graph, the variational energy defines a weighted XY model that, for $\mathbb{Z}_2$ phases, reduces to a classical antiferromagnetic Ising model on that graph. For fixed amplitudes, reconstructing the signs of the ground state wavefunction thus reduces to a weighted Max-Cut instance. This links sign optimization of wavefunctions directly to combinatorial optimization.
item.dc:creator: Mahmud Ashraf Shamim, Md Moshiur Rahman Raj, Mohamed Hibat-Allah, Paulo T Araujo

item.title: Magic and Wormholes in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev Model
item.description: arXiv:2602.12339v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Any quantum state is fully specified by the expectation values of a complete set of Hermitian operators. For a system of Majorana fermions, such as the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model, this set of observables can be taken to be all possible strings of Majorana fermion operators. The expectation values of these fermion strings in a thermal state depend erratically on the microscopic couplings that specify the SYK Hamiltonian, and we study their statistical properties directly in the thermodynamic limit using path integral techniques. When the underlying SYK Hamiltonian is chaotic, we find that these expectation values are well-modeled as real Gaussian random variables with zero mean and a variance that we compute. In contrast, for the integrable variant of SYK, we find that the expectation values are actually non-Gaussian. We then use these results to study measures of magic in the SYK thermal state, including the robustness of magic and the stabilizer R\'enyi entropy. We also show that our results can be quantitatively reproduced with a dual gravity calculation in the chaotic case at sufficiently low temperature. In this dual gravity model the variance of a given microscopic operator string is related to a wormhole geometry stabilized by a massive particle which is dual to the operator string. Our results thus provide a concrete and quantitative setting in which to study the relationship between randomness, wormholes and closed universes, as well as a holographic dual of quantum magic.
item.dc:creator: Val\'erie Bettaque, Brian Swingle

item.title: Gaussian continuous tensor network states: short-distance properties and imaginary-time evolution
item.description: arXiv:2602.15987v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study Gaussian continuous tensor network states (GCTNS) - a finitely parameterized subclass of Gaussian states admitting an interpretation as continuum limits of discrete tensor network states. We show that, at short distance, GCTNS correspond to vacua of free Lifshitz theories with even dynamical exponent, establishing a connection between certain entanglement properties of the two. Two schemes for approximating ground states of free bosonic field theories using GCTNS are presented: rational approximants to the exact dispersion relation and Trotterized imaginary-time evolution. We apply them to Klein-Gordon theory and characterize the resulting GCTNS, identifying the scale at which deviations from its conformal short-distance behavior appear. In particular, we construct an optimal rational approximation for which, at fixed accuracy, the bond dimension grows only logarithmically with the UV cutoff. These results provide a simple and analytically controlled setting to assess the strengths and limitations of GCTNS as variational ans\"atze for relativistic quantum fields.
item.dc:creator: Marco Rigobello, Erez Zohar

item.title: A quadratic Grassmann manifold optimization problem arising from quantum embedding methods
item.description: arXiv:2603.17080v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This article presents a mathematical analysis and numerical strategies for solving the optimization problem of minimizing the quadratic function $J(P) = \text{Tr}(BP)- \frac{1}{2} \text{Tr}(A P A P)$, where $A,B \in \mathbb R^{M \times M}_{\rm sym}$, with $A \succeq 0$, over the Grassmann manifold ${\rm Gr}(m,\mathbb R^M)$. While this problem is non-convex and typically admits non-global local minima - posing challenges for Riemannian optimization and self-consistent field (SCF) algorithms - we identify cases where the global minimizer can be obtained by solving an auxiliary convex problem. When this approach is not directly applicable, the solution to the auxiliary problem still serves as an effective initialization for Riemannian optimization methods and SCF algorithms, significantly improving their performance. This work is motivated by applications in quantum embedding methods, particularly in the construction of bath orbitals, where such optimization problems naturally arise.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Ayral, Eric Canc\`es, Fabian M. Faulstich, Lin Lin, Alicia Negre

item.title: Interplay between photon condensation and electron-electron interactions in molecular systems
item.description: arXiv:2606.11060v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate a minimal molecular model consisting of square planar plaquettes hosting multiple electrons, whose dynamics is governed by a tight-binding Hamiltonian supplemented by on-site Hubbard repulsion. By coupling this system to a spatially nonuniform cavity mode, we analyze the emergence of a magnetostatic instability, namely photon condensation, originating from the paramagnetic Van Vleck mechanism. The global behavior of the system is analyzed for different electronic filling factors, and we find that, except for the special cases of half-filling and a single electron, where the transition, if it occurs, is necessarily a second-order phase transition, the global system may also undergo a first-order transition because of the action of the electron-electron interaction. The polaritonic excitation energies are analyzed, providing clear spectroscopic signatures of the magnetostatic instability and of its order
item.dc:creator: Matteo Parisi, Elisabetta Paladino, Giuseppe A. Falci, Gian Marcello Andolina, Salvatore Savasta, Marco Polini, Francesco M. D. Pellegrino

item.title: Finite-Dimensional Type I von Neumann Algebras in PyTorch: A GPU-Accelerated Framework for Random Block-Diagonal Operators
item.description: arXiv:2606.15882v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: torch_vn_algebra is a PyTorch library for numerical work with finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras, i.e. direct sums of matrix algebras. These algebras are central to operator algebra theory and, via commutants of symmetries, describe quantum systems with conserved charges or superselection rules. To our knowledge, no numerical software treats them as a data type with their centre, family of traces, conditional expectations, inclusions and functional calculus. The library fills the gap between computer algebra (exact but small-scale) and quantum simulators (large-scale but limited to Hilbert-space matrices): it handles batches of operators on CPUs and GPUs with automatic differentiation, and converts operators, states and channels. Key features: Compact tensor representation: 4D tensor (B, C, kmax, kmax), where B is batch size (e.g. Monte Carlo samples), C is the number of summands, and kmax is the max block size, enabling batched GPU processing. Lazy evaluation: matrix data materialized only on access, avoiding memory waste. Random operator generation: custom eigenvalue distributions; Haar, SU(n), COE, CSE unitary ensembles. Functional calculus and spectral methods: matrix absolute value, square root, inverse, entropy via SVD; automatic switch between exact diagonalization (block size up to 256) and power iteration for extreme eigenvalues. Three trace functionals: Tr_blunt (sum of block traces), Tr_norm (dimension-normalized), tau_vN (faithful normal tracial state). Performance: on a Tesla P100 GPU, processing 20,000 samples of 100x100 operators yields up to 30x speedup over traditional CPU workflows. Availability: open-source at https://gitlab.com/a.hobukob/von_neumann_type_i/
item.dc:creator: Irina Nikolaeva, Andrej Novikov

item.title: Multiparameter Quantum Estimation and Degeneracy Structure in Three-Flavor Neutrino Oscillations
item.description: arXiv:2606.30222v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate three-flavor neutrino oscillations within the framework of quantum estimation theory using the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM). We analyze all six independent elements of the QFIM for the parameters $\theta_{23}$, $\delta_{\mathrm{CP}}$, and $\Delta m^2_{31}$, together with the corresponding quantum Cram\'er--Rao bounds and normalized parameter correlations. To connect the intrinsic quantum sensitivity of the neutrino state with experimentally accessible information, we further compare the QFI with the classical Fisher information (CFI) associated with flavor-probability measurements. We find that the difference between the quantum and classical information bounds is strongly dependent on the oscillation parameter and $L/E$, demonstrating that the efficiency with which the available quantum information is accessed depends on the measurement. We also investigate probability-degenerate solutions in the $(\theta_{23},\delta_{\mathrm{CP}})$ parameter space. Although different parameter sets can produce identical $\nu_\mu\rightarrow\nu_e$ appearance probabilities at specific $L/E$ values, their corresponding quantum states can remain distinct, as demonstrated by the quantum fidelity. The QFIM differences further reveal distinct local quantum-information geometries for these probability-degenerate solutions, while the corresponding CFIM differences show a parameter and $L/E$ dependent degree of distinguishability accessible through the flavor-probability measurement. Our results demonstrate that QFI and CFI provide complementary information for neutrino parameter estimation, with the QFIM serving as a measurement-independent quantum benchmark and the CFI characterizing the information accessible through a specified measurement.
item.dc:creator: Bhavna Yadav, Amir Subba, Yu Shi

item.title: Genuine Multi-Entropy in the Toric Code
item.description: arXiv:2607.06050v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study genuine multi-entropy as a diagnostic of multipartite entanglement in the toric code, which provides a controlled setting for probing multipartite structures in topologically ordered states. Our main question is whether genuine multi-entropy captures information that is not reducible to conventional lower-party entropic data, such as topological entanglement entropy. We first analyze toric-code ground states that admit a stabilizer-state description, where the relevant quantities can be evaluated exactly. We conjecture that, for stabilizer states and $\mathtt{q}\ge4$, the $\mathtt{q}$-partite genuine multi-entropy at replica index $n<\mathtt{q}$ collapses to a linear combination of multi-entropies involving at most $\mathtt{q}-2$ parties. We establish this pattern explicitly for $\mathtt{q}=4$ in the toric code stabilizer sector: for $n=2,3$, the genuine multi-entropy is proportional to the tripartite information $I_3$ and, for the Kitaev-Preskill partition, contains no independent genuine four-partite information beyond that captured by the topological entanglement entropy. At $n=4$, however, this reduction breaks down: the genuine multi-entropy is no longer proportional to $I_3$, but remains a topological invariant of the toric-code stabilizer ground states under Kitaev-Preskill-preserving deformations that do not change whether the numbers of vertex- and plaquette-type junctions coincide. For generic non-stabilizer superpositions within the ground-state manifold and for coherent superpositions of local excitations, the low-$n$ reduction also fails. These results show that genuine multi-entropy probes multipartite entanglement structure beyond the tripartite information, and hence beyond the topological entanglement entropy in the Kitaev-Preskill partition, whereas for stabilizer states at low replica index it reduces to lower-partite entropic data.
item.dc:creator: Sriram Akella, Norihiro Iizuka, Akihiro Miyata

item.title: Tunable state-dependent interactions in collisionally stable mixtures of polar molecules
item.description: arXiv:2607.25777v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose encoding a pseudo-spin-$1/2$ system in the ground ($v=0$) and first excited ($v=1$) vibrational states of polar molecules. Double microwave shielding simultaneously shields molecules in both states, suppressing two-body losses by orders of magnitude while strictly avoiding three-body recombination. The microwave dressing is state-dependent and results in highly tunable, long-range dipolar Ising exchange ($J_z$), density-density ($V$), and spin-density ($W$) interactions. These interaction length scales readily exceed the typical interparticle spacing, pushing the molecules deep into the strongly interacting regime. In bulk gases, this enables the exploration of itinerant quantum magnetism and quantum droplets with novel anisotropic spin textures; in optical lattices, it naturally realizes extended Hubbard and $t$-$J_z$ models, opening new directions in quantum simulation.
item.dc:creator: Hubert J. J\'{o}\'{z}wiak, Hanwei Yang, Eugen Dizer, Arthur Christianen, Tijs Karman

item.title: Near-deterministic loading of molecular arrays by microwave-assisted collisions
